questions.question_text: At the start of quiet inhalation, which paired change normally helps draw air into the lungs?
questions.explanation: Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles expands the thorax, lowering lung pressure so air flows inward.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual reference: NCERT Science textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_a: Thoracic volume falls and intrapulmonary pressure rises
questions.option_b: The diaphragm relaxes and the ribs move downward
questions.option_c: The alveoli actively pump air against a pressure gradient
questions.option_d: Thoracic volume rises and intrapulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric pressure

questions.question_text: A patient has fluid accumulating around the alveoli. Which immediate effect is most likely?
questions.explanation: Gas exchange depends on a thin alveolar-capillary barrier. Fluid thickens the diffusion path and can impair oxygen uptake.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual reference: NCERT Science textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_a: Greater diffusion distance impairs oxygen transfer into blood
questions.option_b: Haemoglobin is converted into plasma protein
questions.option_c: The tracheal cartilage rings disappear
questions.option_d: The diaphragm becomes the site of gas exchange

questions.question_text: Why does carbon dioxide generally diffuse from blood into alveolar air?
questions.explanation: Gas exchange is driven by partial-pressure gradients; venous blood arriving at the lungs has a higher carbon-dioxide partial pressure than alveolar air.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual reference: NCERT Science textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_a: Haemoglobin cannot bind any carbon dioxide
questions.option_b: Its partial pressure is higher in blood arriving at the lungs than in alveolar air
questions.option_c: Alveolar walls actively attract carbon dioxide
questions.option_d: Its concentration is always zero in inhaled air

questions.question_text: A blockage in one main bronchus would most directly reduce ventilation to which structure?
questions.explanation: Each main bronchus carries air from the trachea to one lung and branches into smaller airways within it.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual reference: NCERT Science textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_c: The lung on the corresponding side
questions.option_d: The urinary bladder

questions.question_text: During expiration at rest, which event normally occurs after inspiratory muscles relax?
questions.explanation: Elastic recoil and relaxation reduce thoracic volume, slightly raising alveolar pressure above atmospheric pressure and moving air outward.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual reference: NCERT Science textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_a: Thoracic volume increases and alveolar pressure falls
questions.option_b: The ribs are pulled upward by the diaphragm
questions.option_c: Oxygen diffuses from tissues into the alveoli through bone
questions.option_d: Thoracic volume decreases and alveolar pressure rises slightly

questions.question_text: Carbon monoxide exposure is dangerous chiefly because carbon monoxide:
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide forms carboxyhaemoglobin with high affinity, reducing the haemoglobin available to carry oxygen.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual reference: NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_a: Binds haemoglobin strongly and reduces oxygen transport
questions.option_b: Destroys the cartilage rings in the trachea immediately
questions.option_c: Turns alveolar oxygen into nitrogen
questions.option_d: Raises the oxygen-carrying capacity of red cells

questions.question_text: As blood reaches the lungs, oxygenation of haemoglobin promotes release of carbon dioxide. Which effect describes this relationship?
questions.explanation: Oxygenation of haemoglobin in the lungs reduces its capacity to carry carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions, promoting carbon-dioxide unloading (Haldane effect).
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual reference: NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_c: Bainbridge reflex
questions.option_d: Chloride shift

questions.question_text: A rise in blood carbon dioxide normally stimulates breathing primarily through chemoreceptor-driven control of respiratory centres. What is the resulting useful effect?
questions.explanation: Elevated carbon dioxide (largely via increased hydrogen ions) stimulates respiratory control, raising ventilation and helping restore blood-gas balance.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual reference: NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_b: The heart valves reverse their direction
questions.option_c: Ventilation increases to remove more carbon dioxide
questions.option_d: The kidneys stop filtering blood permanently

questions.question_text: A person breathes rapidly at high altitude where atmospheric oxygen pressure is lower. The immediate challenge is reduced oxygen diffusion because:
questions.explanation: Lower inspired oxygen partial pressure reduces alveolar oxygen pressure and the gradient driving diffusion into pulmonary blood.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual reference: NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_c: The trachea becomes a digestive organ
questions.option_d: The alveolar-to-blood oxygen partial-pressure gradient is smaller

questions.question_text: A spirometry report shows a markedly reduced vital capacity. Which quantity does vital capacity represent?
questions.explanation: Vital capacity is the maximum volume that can be exhaled after taking the deepest possible breath.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual reference: NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_a: The greatest volume exhaled after a maximal inhalation
questions.option_b: Air remaining after an ordinary exhalation
questions.option_c: Air exchanged in one quiet breath only
questions.option_d: The volume of blood in pulmonary arteries

questions.question_text: In obstructive asthma, airway narrowing most directly raises resistance to airflow. Which immediate mechanical consequence follows?
questions.explanation: Bronchoconstriction narrows airway lumen and sharply increases resistance, making ventilation more difficult.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual reference: NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_b: More effort is needed to move air, especially during expiration
questions.option_c: The alveolar surface becomes the site of urine formation
questions.option_d: The pulmonary artery changes into a vein

questions.question_text: Why does the pleural fluid layer aid normal breathing?
questions.explanation: The thin pleural fluid layer reduces friction as the lung and chest wall move relative to one another.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual reference: NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_a: It prevents the diaphragm from changing shape
questions.option_b: It digests particles trapped in the bronchi
questions.option_c: It lubricates the pleural surfaces so they can slide with little friction
questions.option_d: It carries oxygen from the nose to the heart

questions.question_text: Damage to airway cilia would most directly weaken which defence?
questions.explanation: Cilia of the conducting airways help move mucus and trapped particles upward for removal.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual reference: NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_c: Exchanging oxygen through the skin
questions.option_d: Moving mucus and trapped particles toward the throat

questions.question_text: Which substance reduces surface tension inside alveoli and helps prevent their collapse, particularly at low lung volumes?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension and increases compliance, helping keep alveoli open.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual reference: NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_c: Bile salt
questions.option_d: Fibrin

questions.question_text: A puncture lets air enter the pleural cavity and the lung recoils inward. This condition is best described as:
questions.explanation: Air in the pleural space can disrupt the pressure coupling that keeps the lung expanded, causing collapse (pneumothorax).
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual reference: NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_c: Emphysema
questions.option_d: Bronchitis

questions.question_text: Which is the usual effect of emphysema on the respiratory surface?
questions.explanation: Emphysema damages alveolar walls and reduces elastic recoil and effective surface area for gas exchange.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual reference: NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_a: The diaphragm is replaced by smooth muscle
questions.option_c: Destruction of alveolar walls reduces effective gas-exchange area
questions.option_d: The trachea develops additional cartilage rings

questions.question_text: The respiratory rhythm is primarily generated and adjusted by centres in which part of the brainstem?
questions.explanation: Brainstem respiratory networks, especially in the medulla with modulation from the pons, regulate breathing rhythm.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; factual reference: NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_c: Spinal ganglia of the legs
questions.option_d: Medulla oblongata and pons

questions.question_text: A person has normal tidal volume and expiratory reserve volume but a sharply reduced inspiratory reserve volume. Which measurement is directly reduced?
questions.explanation: Inspiratory capacity is tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume; reducing the latter lowers inspiratory capacity.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; fact checked against NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_c: Functional residual capacity
questions.option_d: Anatomical dead space

questions.question_text: After a normal expiration, a person still has air in the lungs. Which volume includes this remaining air together with expiratory reserve volume?
questions.explanation: Functional residual capacity is the volume remaining after a normal expiration: residual volume plus expiratory reserve volume.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; fact checked against NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_c: Functional residual capacity
questions.option_d: Inspiratory capacity

questions.question_text: A restrictive lung disorder makes the lungs stiff. Which mechanical change is expected for a given inspiratory pressure?
questions.explanation: Compliance is change in volume per change in pressure; stiff lungs have reduced compliance and expand less for a given pressure.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; fact checked against NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_a: No change in expansion at any pressure
questions.option_c: Higher lung compliance and easier expansion
questions.option_d: Lower lung compliance and smaller expansion

questions.question_text: A person rapidly breathes off excessive carbon dioxide during a panic episode. Which immediate acid-base shift is expected?
questions.explanation: Acute hyperventilation lowers arterial carbon dioxide, reducing carbonic acid and raising blood pH (respiratory alkalosis).
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; fact checked against NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_a: Respiratory acidosis as blood carbon dioxide rises
questions.option_b: Metabolic alkalosis from bicarbonate loss in urine
questions.option_c: No pH change because carbon dioxide is not involved
questions.option_d: Respiratory alkalosis as blood carbon dioxide falls

questions.question_text: Why can a pulmonary embolus lower oxygenation even when air reaches the affected alveoli?
questions.explanation: An embolus blocks perfusion to ventilated regions, creating high ventilation-perfusion mismatch and wasted ventilation.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; fact checked against NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_a: Some ventilated alveoli receive too little perfusion for effective gas exchange
questions.option_c: The diaphragm cannot contract at all
questions.option_d: Haemoglobin stops binding oxygen throughout the body

questions.question_text: Anatomic dead space refers chiefly to air that:
questions.explanation: Conducting airways such as the trachea and bronchi conduct air but do not themselves provide alveolar gas exchange.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; fact checked against NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_a: Is exchanged between blood and body cells
questions.option_b: Remains in conducting passages and does not directly exchange gases
questions.option_c: Is trapped in the pleural cavity
questions.option_d: Is bound to haemoglobin

questions.question_text: A standard spirometer records forced expiration but cannot directly measure which volume because it remains in the lungs after maximal expiration?
questions.explanation: Residual volume remains after maximal forced expiration, so it cannot be measured by simple spirometry alone.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; fact checked against NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_c: Residual volume
questions.option_d: Expiratory reserve volume

questions.question_text: Which respiratory change is most characteristic of a bronchodilator acting on airway smooth muscle?
questions.explanation: Relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle widens airway lumens and reduces resistance, improving airflow.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; fact checked against NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_a: Alveolar walls thicken and diffusion stops
questions.option_b: The pleural cavity fills with air
questions.option_c: Haemoglobin is removed from red cells
questions.option_d: Airway radius increases and resistance to airflow falls

questions.question_text: A shallow breath may ventilate conducting airways without adequately renewing alveolar air. Which quantity best captures this limitation?
questions.explanation: Alveolar ventilation is the fresh air reaching gas-exchanging regions per unit time, excluding dead-space ventilation.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; fact checked against NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_c: Pulmonary blood volume
questions.option_d: Vital capacity alone

questions.question_text: During strenuous exercise, increased carbon dioxide and hydrogen-ion levels in active tissues favour oxygen unloading from haemoglobin. Which principle explains this shift?
questions.explanation: Higher carbon dioxide and lower pH reduce haemoglobin affinity for oxygen, facilitating unloading in metabolically active tissues.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; fact checked against NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_c: Haldane effect only in the lungs
questions.option_d: Frank-Starling law

questions.question_text: At pulmonary capillaries, oxygen enters blood from alveolar air; at systemic capillaries, oxygen leaves blood for tissues. These two exchanges are respectively called:
questions.explanation: External respiration is gas exchange at the lungs; internal respiration is exchange between systemic blood and tissues.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; fact checked against NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_c: Ventilation and cellular respiration
questions.option_d: Inspiration and expiration

questions.question_text: In red cells at systemic tissues, chloride ions move into the cell as bicarbonate moves out. What is this exchange associated with?
questions.explanation: The chloride shift maintains electrical neutrality as bicarbonate formed from tissue carbon dioxide exits red cells.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; fact checked against NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_c: Conversion of urea into ammonia
questions.option_d: Transport of carbon dioxide in blood (chloride shift)

questions.question_text: Particles that reach the alveolar region, beyond the ciliated conducting airways, are removed principally by which cells?
questions.explanation: Alveolar macrophages phagocytose particles and microbes that reach the distal air spaces.
questions.source: Original SSC-level practice; fact checked against NCERT Biology textbook portal https://ncert.nic.in/textbook.php
questions.option_c: Type I pneumocytes
questions.option_d: Red blood cells
